comment: Hand-authored Daily Loop seed clue sets. 12 famous, guessable places, one per clue file, in this exact order -> clues/{index}.json (0..11). Each clues array is positional: [geography, climate, history, hook, giveaway]. Guardrails: every clue <= 40 words, grade 4-6 reading level; NEVER the place name, demonym, old name, or country/region name in ANY clue; NEVER the eponym in clues 1-3 (listed under eponyms); tier 5 is a landmark giveaway, not a summary. 'banned' applies to all 5 clues (word-boundary match); single banned words >= 4 chars are also rejected when embedded inside another token.

clues: A grand old capital bends around a wide river flowing northwest to the sea, set on a low plain of chalk hills and farmland.
Winters are gray and damp but rarely freeze hard; ocean winds that soften the cold also dump the heaviest rains in late autumn.
Legionaries built a riverside town here two thousand years ago; a great cathedral rose on the island, and a stormed fortress lit a revolution.
A tower built for a world fair was meant to stand just twenty years — locals hated it at first, and now the world can't picture the city without it.
The Eiffel Tower — the iron lattice icon finished in 1889 — rises on the river's left bank.
The world's largest city rings a deep bay on the east coast of a long island nation, backed by mountains and a perfect cone volcano to the west.
Summers are hot, sticky, and lashed by typhoons; winters turn dry and bright as cold winds blow in off the mainland — snow is rare.
A fishing village grew around a warlord's castle from 1603; after 1868 the emperor moved in and the castle town became the nation's capital.
Its dawn fish market once sold more tuna before sunrise than most ports sell all day, and its subway carries more riders daily than some nations' railways.
In the old riverside district stands the city's oldest temple, entered through a gate hung with a giant red paper lantern.
A megacity crowds both banks of a great river flowing north through the desert, just above where the river fans into a wide green delta.
Some years see no rain at all — yet each spring a hot dust wind roars off the desert, pushing past forty degrees and choking the streets.
A conquering army founded it in 641 beside an old river fortress; it grew rich on the trade road between two seas and raised a thousand minarets.
Its museum once held a boy king's solid-gold funeral mask, found untouched in a small tomb cut into the southern desert cliffs.
The Pyramids of Giza — the last surviving wonder of the ancient world — stand on the desert plateau at the city's edge.
A harbor city wraps around a drowned river valley on the southeast coast of a vast island continent, its surf beaches facing the open ocean.
Summer afternoons can be shattered by a 'southerly buster' — a cold front racing up the coast that drops the temperature ten degrees in an hour.
A fleet of convict ships landed in 1788 at a sheltered cove, and the rough penal colony grew into the continent's oldest and largest city.
Sailors call it the finest natural harbor on earth, and its New Year's Eve fireworks are the first great show the planet sees each year.
White sail-shaped shells rise over the harbor point — the opera house with the most famous roof in the world.
A city of granite peaks and crescent beaches curls around a great bay on the Atlantic, where forested mountains drop straight into the sea.
Summer rain falls in warm afternoon bursts that steam off the stone peaks; winter is the dry, golden season, when the beaches fill.
Gold fleets made it a colonial capital in 1763, and for thirteen years it was the only city in the Americas to host a European royal court.
Each year its carnival parade fills a purpose-built avenue with drummers and dancers in feathers — the biggest street party on earth.
Christ the Redeemer spreads his arms over the city from the peak of Corcovado.
Five boroughs crowd islands and riverbanks where a great tidal estuary meets the ocean, at the mouth of a river running south through a mountain gap.
Summers are sweltering and humid, winters can bury the streets in snow — and ocean hurricanes sometimes climb the coast and flood the subways.
A trading post swapped for trinkets in 1626 changed flags, became a new nation's first capital, then the door through which millions entered.
Its harbor holds a torch-bearing statue that was a gift from across the ocean, and a glittering ball drops in its famous square every New Year's Eve.
The Statue of Liberty lifts her torch in the harbor.
A capital straddles a tidal river winding east to a wide estuary, on a low plain where chalk hills meet clay in the southeast of a rainy island.
It rains a little all year but rarely pours — the famous 'fogs' were coal smoke, and in past centuries the river froze solid enough for fairs.
Legionaries bridged the river here two thousand years ago; a great tower fortress rose a thousand years later, and a great fire cleared the medieval streets.
Ravens are still kept in its ancient fortress — legend says the kingdom falls if they leave — and its guards wear tall bearskin hats.
Big Ben's tower chimes over the river beside the parliament halls.
A vast capital spreads over a dry northern plain, ringed by mountains on three sides, near the old corridor that leads west to the steppe.
Winters are bitter, bone-dry, and dust-blown off the deserts; summers turn hot and wet when the monsoon finally pushes this far north.
Steppe khans built their capital here in the 1200s; later emperors raised a walled palace city at its heart that stood for five centuries.
Its main square is the largest public square on earth, and a wall twenty-one thousand kilometers long snakes over the mountains just north of town.
The Forbidden City's golden roofs still fill the old center, ringed by its great red walls.
A capital stands on a winding river in the heart of a vast flat plain, where mixed forest fades into farmland, far from any sea.
Winter can plunge past minus thirty and drag on for months; summer answers with a short blast of heat past thirty-five — a sixty-five-degree swing.
A wooden hill fort grew into a princes' seat, survived a great invasion from the east, and became the heart of an empire touching two oceans.
Its fortress square holds a cathedral of candy-colored onion domes, and its subway stations look like underground palaces.
St. Basil's candy-striped domes rise over the great square at the city's very center.
A city squeezes between a flat-topped mountain and the sea at the southwestern tip of a continent, where two oceans nearly meet.
It rains in winter here, not summer — the one corner of its country with that flipped pattern — while a fierce summer southeaster scrubs the air clean.
A supply garden planted by passing ships in 1652 grew into its country's oldest city, a halfway house on the long sea road to the east.
Its mountain wears a 'tablecloth' of cloud that spills over the flat top, and penguins waddle across its suburban beaches.
Table Mountain's flat top looms over the harbor.
A megacity packs seven old islands, now joined into one, along a narrow coastal strip facing a wide western sea, with forested hills behind.
One summer monsoon dumps most of the year's rain in about four months — streets can flood waist-deep — then eight dry months follow.
Handed over as a royal dowry in 1661, it grew from trading port to mill town to the commercial heart of its subcontinent by 1900.
Its film studios release more movies per year than any other city on earth, and its lunch couriers deliver two hundred thousand home-cooked meals a day.
The triumphal stone arch on the waterfront, built for a visiting king, still frames the old harbor.
A megacity fills a high mountain basin more than two kilometers above the sea, ringed by volcanoes where a great lake once shimmered.
At this height the sun burns by day but nights stay cool all year — and the rainy season fires a thunderstorm nearly every afternoon.
An island city of canals and causeways stood here until 1521; the conquerors drained the lake and raised their churches on its stones.
Its great square sits over a buried temple, and the whole city is slowly sinking as the old lakebed settles beneath it.
The great cathedral and the national palace face each other across one of the world's largest plazas.
